paper_title: CUAWright: A Minimal Unified Interface for Digital Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The prevailing approach to computer-use agents couples a model with a domain-specific harness: a browser or desktop environment equipped with human engineered tools that are fixed before task execution. As models' coding capabilities improve, the GUI native and static harness prevents them from direct programmatic operation on system state, as well as flexible construction of tools. To this end, we introduce CUAWright, a minimal terminal harness of roughly 3K lines of code that uses bash commands as its sole action interface, and a file system as its evolvable space for dynamically creating tools and managing the context. We conduct comprehensive experiments across a wide range of digital tasks, and demonstrate that by giving the agent a minimal, programmable interface, it achieves substantially stronger results compared to their GUI or hybrid CLI interface across a wide range of tasks. On OSWorld 2.0, CUAWright delivers a 33.2% relative improvement in partial reward while reducing estimated cost by 37.5% compared with the published GPT-5.5 baseline. On Online-Mind2Web and the long horizon Odysseys benchmark, CUAWright substantially outperforms GUI native harness by 4.7% and 44.0% in success rate, respectively. Furthermore, we found the gains extend to CAD applications that require accurate visual understanding and CLI interaction: on CADGenBench and BenchCAD, our unified harness yields 8.1%-41.6% relative improvements over other CLI based harnesses with GPT-5.5. Together, these results suggest digital environments are far more programmable than their GUI interfaces imply, and a minimal terminal-focused harness is the key for better performance and efficiency.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Computer-use agents have advanced rapidly across different domains and tasks. Web agents can observe screenshots or DOM tree of web pages at each step, and select the next elements or predict pixel coordinates to operate on directly (Deng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Pahuja et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2026; Awadallah et al., 2026). Similarly, desktop agents can use softwares in the environments through screenshots and low-level mouse and keyboard actions like humans (Xie et al., 2024; Bonatti et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Agashe et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). However, solving computer-use tasks through stepwise screenshot or accessibility observations and low level actions is limiting since the screenshot exposes limited information of the environment state. And primitive actions associated with keyboard and mouse movements constrains the agent from direct and programmatic access to the underlying system state. More recent works explored hybrid interfaces that delegate GUI operation and code action through different sub-agents (Song et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2026) or explicitly define tool to execute code against the environment (Parikh et al., 2026). However, they are domain-specific and GUI centric, where agents are restricted to fixed set of predefined tools. Work done during an internship at Microsoft Research.

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: Figure 1: CUAWright demonstrates strong performance across different digital task benchmarks. For each benchmark, we compare CUAWright with the existing GUI or hybrid CLI based approach with highest performance score using the same underlying model. CUAWright demonstrated substantially better performance compared to the baselines. To address the above challenges, we propose terminal native harness in which every model action is terminal command. As shown in Figure 2, at each step the agent model predicts an action in command line interface to engage with the underlying execution environment, which consists of runtime, file system and an expandable set of tools and libraries. In particular, browser task is driven by agent generated code written against the debugging protocol (Microsoft, 2025); desktop task is driven naturally through terminal command, CLI tools, or directly editing the source file. When surface genuinely prevents programmatic control, the agent uses keyboard and mouse actions through xdotool/pyautogui command. Therefore CUAWright features: 1) single terminal action space that is universal, allowing agent to interact with both system state and keyboard and mouse actions, and 2) direct and programmatic access to file system that the agent can use to manage its context, and craft new tools through writing, testing and executing program files using terminal commands. Further, in contrast to GUI native and hybrid harnesses which append screenshot at every step, CUAWrights default observation is terminal output, and the agent captures screenshot on demand. We summarize our contributions into the following: We introduce CUAWright, minimal harness in which agents perform web and desktop tasks solely through terminal commands, and use file system for context management and new tool creation. We evaluate CUAWright across live and long-horizon web, desktop, and computer aided design (CAD) tasks, and show that terminal-centric interaction is effective, efficient, and substantially more robust than GUI native or hybrid interaction. We conduct extensive ablation studies between single agent and multi-agent settings when using terminal native harness, and demonstrate that the file system is crucial for the performance. Detailed analysis shows emergent behaviors of frontier models crafting its own creative tools and reuse them within the task.

sections.title: 2 METHOD
sections.content: Formulation.

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: Figure 2: The CUAWright architecture. Terminal serves as the sole interface between the agent and the task environment. At each step of task execution process, the agent model receives command line output as observation or call CLI tool to load image into context on demand, and output commands that gets executed. The underlying execution environment contains runtime, an expandable set of installed CLI tools and applications, and file system as the agents workspace to programmatically manage system state and craft new tools. We formulate the digital agent task as partially observable Markov decision process with environment state space S, observation space O, terminal action space Aterm, and transition function . Given natural-language task , the agent interacts with digital environment E, such as web browser, desktop application, or CAD system, to accomplish the task. At step t, the environment is in state st and provides an observation ot produced by the preceding terminal execution, where ot defaults to textual output from terminal. When necessary, the agent can call predefined CLI tool to load images into its context so that ot can also contain visual information. Conditioned on , ot, and the interaction history ht = {(oi, ai)}i<t, the agent produces an executable terminal action at = π(T, ot, ht), at Aterm. Executing at induces the transition st+1 = TE (st, at) and produces the next observation ot+1. We decompose the environment state as st = (xt, ft), where xt denotes the underlying application and system state, and ft denotes the persistent filesystem state, including the agent workspace and artifacts created during interaction. Unlike conventional computer-use harnesses based on GUI primitives or domain-specific APIs, CUAWright uses executable terminal commands as unified action interface. The action space Aterm remains fixed across task domains and environments, while enabling the agent to directly access and manipulate system state and dynamically construct task-specific tools. Vision on demand, not by default. CUAWright instead keeps visual input optional: ot contains only the output produced by executing the terminal action at. This design substantially reduces cost compared with conventional interactive agent paradigms (e.g., roughly one-third of the cost on OSWorld 2); see Section 3.2 for details. Persistent workspace as external state. Let wt ft denote the portion of the filesystem assigned to the agent as its local workspace. Filesystem modifications produced by terminal commands persist across interaction steps, inducing workspace trajectory w0, w1, . . . , wn. CUAWright introduces no separate memory state and no memory-specific interface. Instead, information that the agent wishes to retain can be externalized directly into wt, including extracted values, intermediate results, task progress, logs, or records of previous failures. Memory operations are therefore ordinary terminal actions. The agent may create, read, search, append to, reorganize, or delete files using the same action space Aterm used to manipulate the external application. If an artifact becomes inaccurate or obsolete, the agent can modify or remove it rather than accumulating an immutable interaction history. The workspace is also independent of the models active context window: files remain available after context compaction and can be explicitly read again when needed. Dynamic tool construction in the workspace. The same workspace also serves as substrate for constructing new executable capabilities during task execution. Let Pt = Penv Pagent(wt), where Penv contains programs initially supplied by the execution environment and Pagent(wt) contains executable artifacts created by the agent in its workspace. Through ordinary terminal actions, the agent can write script or program into wt, execute it, inspect its output, revise its implementation, and subsequently invoke it with new arguments. Once executable through the terminal, the artifact becomes part of the agents effective program set Pt. For example, if task repeatedly requires an operation that is inconvenient to express through existing programs, the agent may first implement that operation as parameterized command-line program and then reuse it in later steps. This allows procedures discovered during interaction to be materialized as executable artifacts that can be directly tested, revised, and reused (Wang et al., 2024a;b; Zheng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025).

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate CUAWright on six benchmarks across web, desktop, and computer aided design (CAD), covering wide set of high value digital task domains. 3.1 WEB APPLICATIONS: ONLINE-MIND2WEB AND ODYSSEYS Online-Mind2Web (Xue et al., 2025) is widely adopted benchmark to assess the performance of web agents on live real websites. It includes 300 tasks spanning 136 popular websites across diverse domains, with an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator for assessing task completion. We evaluated the performance of the GPT-5.4 using CUAWright on the full 300-task OnlineMind2Web benchmark. To make it compatible with the original eval settings, we enforce the agent to save critical point screenshots and to log actions during the run through prompting. We follow the official automated evaluation protocol and report the performance. We also compare against the GPT-5.4 baseline in conventional screenshot-based agent setting reported in (Awadallah et al., 2026), where the model predicts x,y coordinates for clicks and typing actions. Using the same underlying model, CUAWright delivers substantial improvements in medium and hard level tasks, with particularly on hard tasks, demonstrating the advantage of code-driven, terminal-based approach over step-by-step coordinate prediction. Odysseys (Jang et al., 2026b) is web agent benchmark designed to evaluate agents on realistic, long-horizon browsing tasks that involve sustained planning, memory, and cross-page reasoning spanning diverse websites. All runs are evaluated on 105 of the 108 public tasks with maximum of 300 steps. We exclude tasks 026 and 041, which require an unavailable GitLab server, and task 082, which requires nested Docker and is not reliably supported by our evaluation setup. As shown in Table 2, CUAWright achieves 63.2% with GPT-5.5 xhigh and 67.9% with GPT-5.6 Sol Max in the single-agent setting, significantly outperforming the corresponding official leaderboard baselines. Further, we conducted two ablation studies on the effect of single v.s. multi-agent and the effect of file system in section 3.6.1. CUAWrights terminal-first approach represents the frontier for performance/cost optimality. As shown in Figure 3, with GPT-5.5 xhigh, CUAWright improves the performance by 15.7 points over the corresponding OpenAI baseline while reducing the cost by $6.0 per task. With GPT-5.6 Sol Max, it improves the partial score by 5.2 points while reducing the per-task cost by approximately $9.5. 3.3 LONG-HORIZON DESKTOP AND APPLICATION TASKS: WEAVEBENCH WeaveBench complements OSWorld with 114 long-horizon tasks across eight work domains, requiring GUI observation and CLI or code execution within one trajectory. WeaveBench trajectories 2OpenAI introduced promotional pricing for GPT-5.6 Sol on August 21, 2026, reducing the API price from $5/$30 to $4/$20 per million input/output tokens. Using the pre-promotion pricing, CUAWright with GPT-5.6 Sol costs $5.7 per task, still substantially below the leaderboard reported cost of $13.9 per task.

Single agents. Previous studies have shown benefits of multi-agent architecture for GUI native and hybrid interfaces (Song et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026), we study the effect of multi-agent in terminal native CUAWright harness. In the docker environment, Penv we install 2 new independent sub agents as CLI tool that the main terminal agent can call: 1) planner agent, instructed to make plan and create criteria for the self-verification before submission, 2) self-verification agent, instructed to verify whether the task is completed given the traces and the criteria provided by the planner agent.

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: The results in table 2 show that single agent performs as well as the multiagent settings. We show two representative examples in Appendix A.6 demonstrating one case here multi-agent helps and another where single agent is better. Through careful manual review of the agent traces, we found that for OS World tasks, the planner agent often struggles to create accurate success criteria for the agent to self verify its own answer before submission. And we found that frontier models like GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol already learns the behavior of verifying its own answer even without standalone verifier agent. In addition, we find that the multi-agent setting substantially increases the median number of task turns: from 101 to 151 for GPT-5.6-sol, and from 73 to 137 for GPT-5.5. 2 Ablation 2: With v.s. without file system. As the file system is core component of CUAWright, enabling the agent not only to directly manipulate files, but also to maintain persistent memory and create reusable tools during execution, we conduct an ablation study to assess its contribution. Specifically, we explicitly enforce no direct programmatic file system operations such as checking, editing and creating files using terminal command through prompting (exact prompt used can be found in Appendix A.3). The agent can still modify files indirectly through GUI operations using mouse and keyboard actions with xdotool/pyautogui CLI tool. As shown in the table 2, restricting the agent from programmatic access to file system leads to significant decrease in the performance of GPT 5.6 Sol (-12.1 pts). This suggests that programmatic control is essential to terminal-native harness. 3.6.2 QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS 3 Can agents craft their own tools during task execution to improve efficiency? One benefit of CUAWright is that it offers local workspace where the agent can create tools during task execution, and reuse them. In OSWorld 2 evaluation, we found in 89 (84.8%) tasks the GPT-5.6 Sol agent explicitly created at least one saved code or executable-like file. In total there are 776 executable files created, where 192 (24.7%) were reused (appeared in at least two distinct execution-command events). The created tools focus on inspection and extraction, interface automation, Artifact construction/editing and verification/testing. The figure 5 in the Appendix shows for task 005, the user needs to go through the files on Desktop and find the medical records related to 2024 medical visits and personal information. The agent first crafts new tool to group all image files into single composite image, and extracts all needed information at once, instead of individually check each image to see if it is related to medical information and gather results, which is much more efficient than GUI based approach. 4 How far can agents go without relying on primitive actions? We classify task as Terminal-only when the actions contain no xdotool, pyautogui, or equivalent operating-system input invocation. And found that tasks that are terminal only performs significantly better than mixed terminal and GUI operation tasks. For examples, Terminal-only includes Conda/pip setup and browser automation without OS input. Mixed includes dinosaur-game keypresses, puzzle drags, and traces that use xdotool only to focus or verify an application. GPT-5.5 most frequently misread the task (19.4%), whereas GPT-5.6 Sol was more affected by outputs that appeared correct but lacked sufficient precision (19.0%). sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Web and desktop interaction. Early web agent interacts with the browser through structured elements such as DOM (Yao et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; de Chezelles et al., 2025), with screenshot as visual context (Koh et al., 2024; Drouin et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2026b), while WebVoyager and SeeAct ground multimodal decisions on live websites (He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). While for desktop agents, majority of works treat mouse, and keyboard as universal interface (Zheng et al., 2024; Shaw et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024; Bonatti et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Jang et al., 2026a). More recently, Qwen-UI-Agent unifies GUI actions with CLI execution and batched actions across mobile, desktop, and web environments (Zhou et al., 2026). However, these interaction paradigms remain tied either to environment specific representations or repeated low-level visual grounding. Also in Yuan et al. (2026), the authors found that recent frontier models increasingly favor programmatic actions even in GUI-native action space. Our design takes step further: we set terminal command to be the only primary model action, and GUI control is invoked programmatically, and used as fallback rather than being the dominant action space. Code-first and hybrid alternatives. The closest work increasingly acts on program state rather than pixels. CoAct-1 delegates between GUI operator and programmer agent, reducing brittle interaction chains through Python and Bash actions (Song et al., 2026). Screenshots or Tools? studies GUIMCP routing and finds that providing programmatic tools does not ensure that agents will adopt them effectively (Fan et al., 2026). StateAct makes program state primary, uses GUI specialists only where needed, and verifies persisted outputs with an independent completion gate (Yang et al., 2026). StructAgent addresses complementary problem by maintaining compact, verifier-backed causal representation of progress for checkpointing and recovery (Wu et al., 2026). Most directly, Terminal Agents Suffice shows that terminal-and-filesystem coding agent can outperform GUIand MCP-based alternatives on enterprise platforms by writing code against their APIs (Bechard et al., 2026). Our work shares this terminal-first motivation but studies broader claim: whether one command action space and filesystem context can support live-web, desktop, and graphical application tasks, including settings that are not reducible to enterprise APIs.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced CUAWright, minimal harness that gives the agent bash as its sole action interface and the file system as workspace for directly operating on system state and building new tools. We conducted comprehensive experiments on six benchmarks covering wide range of digital tasks including web, desktop and CAD applications. CUAWright demonstrated that universal terminal interface improves both the performance and cost efficiency of computer-use agents compared with GUI-only and hybrid interfaces supported by domain-specific harnesses. As frontier LLMs rapidly advance in coding and vision, we expect computer-use agents to increasingly benefit from unified, terminal-only interface that enables seamless operation across code and low level action spaces.

sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS One important limitation of CUAWright is that directly modifying the underlying system state may introduce additional risks. Agent actions that change files, configurations, application state, or other persistent resources can have unintended or irreversible side effects, especially when the agent operates with incomplete observations or makes an incorrect decision. Such modifications also raise practical questions around permission control, state consistency, rollback, and recovery from failed actions. In this work, we therefore focus primarily on interaction and execution under controlled settings, and leave robust mechanisms for safe state modificationsuch as transactional execution, validation, sandboxing, and automatic rollbackto future work. A.

sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: For web benchmarks Online-Mind2Web and Odysseys, CUAWright runs its workspace on the host and executes each command with the system shell under per-command timeout, with interactive pagers disabled. Observations are truncated at twenty-four thousand characters, the transcript is compacted every twenty steps, and run is capped at one hundred steps. For desktop tasks, CUAWright runs each task in container-hosted Ubuntu virtual machine provided by the OSWorld 2.0 environment (Yuan et al., 2026), with hardware acceleration where available, and reaches it through the guest execution endpoint. Commands are capped at three hundred seconds and their output at sixteen thousand characters, retained as head and tail around an explicit truncation notice so that both the beginning and the end of long output survive. run is capped at three hundred model steps in total across all roles. Final detailed cost for CUAWright single agent settings is in Table 7. Table 7: OSWorld 2.0 evaluation statistics and cost comparison. Metric GPT-5.5 xhigh GPT-5.6 Sol max Tasks scored Partial score Exact passes Input tokens Output tokens Total tokens Current Standard cost Cost per task 105/105 63.2242% 27/105 400,638,827 14,967,422 415,606,249 $1,054.93 $10.05 105/105 67.9130% 29/105 434,755,823 4,394,423 439,150,246 $458.93 $4.37 A.3 PROMPT FOR ABLATION STUDY OF FILESYSTEM Below is the prompt we used to enforce no filesystem related operations. You are Actor in an Ubuntu desktop VM. Complete the task, verify the result, and submit. Treat the task instruction as the central, top-level requirement. Follow its exact wording, named application, requested result, and restrictions. First, re-read the instruction. As general guide, inventory whichever parts of the task-relevant environment are useful, such as open applications, documents, browser tabs, accounts, and files in locations like Desktop, Downloads, and Documents. Let the task context determine the method and scope. Inspect any source or reference that must be matched. If required file or fact is missing, ask the user one concise question.

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: Use run_command for commands, automation, application control, and inspection. Filesystem restriction: - Do not use run_command to perform filesystem writes or changes directly. Before running command, consider whether it would change filesystem state. - Do not use cat or sed with redirection, shell editing tools, Python file APIs, or similar command-line strategies to make filesystem changes. Read-only inspection and in-memory or stdout analysis remain allowed. - Make required changes through the named application's GUI or other user-facing controls, using xdotool, CDP, or accessibility as appropriate. Normal Open, Save, Save As, Import, Export, and browser-download actions triggered through the GUI are allowed. - temporary screenshot created solely for the immediately following image_show.py call is allowed. - Reuse the application, browser instance, profile, document, and state opened by setup. - Use the application and output format named in the task. - Complete every explicit requirement and avoid unrelated changes. - Prefer minimal edits and exact typed values. - Save, export, send, upload, or download to the exact requested destination. - For GIMP, do not save or export unless explicitly requested. Verify the final result directly: - visual result: inspect full-size screenshot; - exact value or property: read it back; - file or document: reopen the saved artifact; - web action: reload and confirm the resulting record; - behavior: exercise it and confirm the state change. If verification finds defect, repair it and verify again. Stop when the task is complete. Tools: - Image: `python /opt/cuawright-tools/image_show.py --path ABSOLUTE_PATH` - Ask user: `python /opt/cuawright-tools/ask_user.py --question "TEXT"` - Submit: `python /opt/cuawright-tools/submit.py` Run `/opt/cuawright-tools/*.py` tool as the only command in its run_command call. Browser: - Use the existing Chrome instance and profile. - Connect at `http://127.0.0.1:1337` with `/home/user/.local/share/osw/venv/bin/python`. - Prefer `Accessibility.getFullAXTree` to inspect controls and state. - Use CDP, xdotool, screenshots, keyboard, and mouse to operate user-facing controls. When complete and verified, run submit.py. A.4 QUALITATIVE EXAMPLES OF CUAWRIGHT ON DIFFERENT BENCHMARKS A.4.1 WEAVEBENCH: DIAGNOSING CHECKOUT LATENCY INCIDENT The following trace shows the same mechanism applied across broader systems diagnosis. In WeaveBench task DAV task 17 jaeger trace root cause compare, the agent was asked to identify the source of checkout latency incident and leave reproducible evidence bundle. The

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: Figure 5: Tool-crafted batched visual inspection in Task005. The agent writes and executes lightweight sheet() utility in the terminal (left), combining 13 JPEG documents into one filenameannotated contact sheet (center). single multimodal inspection replaces repeated GUI-based image opening and produces structured response grouping the medical evidence by visit date, diagnosis, expenses, and supporting files (right). task required raw Jaeger exports, latency distribution, slow trace and its longest leaf span, an OTLP packet capture, four native Jaeger screenshots, hypothesis, and root-cause report. The first API request failed because port 16685 spoke HTTP/0.9 rather than the expected Jaeger HTTP API. The agent probed the neighboring service, found the working endpoint on port 16686, and continued from observed state rather than repeating the original assumption. It then queried the service and operation indexes, generated additional real traces with the provided emitter, exported 190 POST /checkout traces, reconstructed their parentchild relationships, and computed the root-span distribution. The resulting median was 116.857 ms, while p95 and p99 were 3361.620 ms and 3558.904 ms, respectively. The agent did not stop at the programmatic diagnosis. It used tcpdump on the collector port while replaying the real emitter, launched Chrome against the Jaeger UI, navigated to the selected slow trace, expanded the bottleneck span, and opened fast-versus-slow comparison. It inspected each screenshot before submission and wrote report that separated detection from attribution: RED metrics established that checkout was slow, while the trace waterfall localized the delay to the downstream payments gateway. The report recommended fail-fast timeout, circuit breaking around repeated 504 responses, controlled fallback behavior, dependency ownership, and trace-based regression gates. The trajectory used 45 model calls and 45 terminal commands over approximately 26.6 minutes. It received final WeaveBench score of 0.93875. Machine-readable exports, the packet capture, and the written diagnosis were fully correct. The remaining deductions were mostly presentational: the search screenshot did not isolate perfectly clean slow cluster, and the comparison view was merged difference graph rather than the evaluators preferred strict side-by-side layout. This example exercises environment discovery, API use, statistical analysis, packet capture, browser automation, visual inspection, causal diagnosis, and technical communication within one trajectory. The receipts were in MailHub inbox, the charges could be cross-checked in VaultBank account, and the claim had to follow written guideline and the particulars of previously submitted report. Instead of opening each e-mail and each bank search in the GUI, the agent wrote two tools: an 18-line mail open info.py that opens an e-mail by its exact subject and prints its body and attachments, and 12-line vault search.py that types query into the banks

The agent first exports and analyzes the Jaeger traces programmatically, then drives the native UI to verify the causal path visually. The slowtrace waterfall (left) shows payments.gateway.http occupying almost the full 4.12-second checkout request. Expanding that leaf span (right) reads back the decisive evidence: HTTP 504, OpenTelemetry ERROR, an upstream timeout, and peer.service=payments-gateway. transaction search and prints the matching rows. It then called them 13 times, once per supporting e-mail and once per charge, and reconciled every receipt against bank posting. The trajectory used 167 model calls and 163 terminal commands over approximately 117 minutes and received final OSWorld-V2 score of 0.8816; the evaluator does not itemize the deduction. As in the previous traces, the agent verified by readback rather than by trust: it noticed that the review page showed the expense range as 02-DEC-2025 21-NOV-2025 because the application sorts date strings lexicographically, recorded this as display defect, and left the claim data untouched. A.4.3 OSWORLD-V2: FIXING AN AWS BILLING ANOMALY WITHOUT SINGLE SCREENSHOT In task 070, PI asks in TeamChat for an abnormal AWS bill to be investigated, fixed in the (mock) console, and summarized back in the channel. The lab policy allows $3,000 per month in two approved regions. The agent switched into the lab-admin role, read the Billing page ($11,462 month-to-date against the $3,000 budget), and found the cause in eu-west-1: four p4d.24xlarge instances and four 2 TB io2 volumes. For the remaining console work it wrote 37-line cdp click.py (on top of 115-line CDP helper) that resolves an accessibility name, role, or node id in the live accessibility tree, reads the elements box model, and clicks its center. It then invoked the script 15 more times, each call single line with new argument, to delete the volumes, deactivate the interns access key, and post the incident update. Every observation in this trajectory was the accessibility tree or page text printed to stdout. It used 69 model calls and 68 terminal commands over approximately 20 minutes and received final OSWorld-V2 score of 1.0. A.5 BENCHCAD: RECONSTRUCTING HEAT SINK We illustrate how CUAWright performs on CAD tasks using the BenchCAD Vision2Code record heat sink 003731 s20260505, officially classified as hard on scale of easy to hard. The agent received four views of the heat-sink part and had to write CadQuery code that reproduced its 3D geometry. The submitted STEP file is scored by voxel intersection-over-union (IoU), from 0 to 1. CUAWright follows an iterative workflow: write CadQuery code, render the result, evaluate it against the reference views, and revise the code. This is analogous to the tool-enabled BenchCAD settings reported by OpenAI and Anthropic because the model can use execution feedback to improve its answer. It differs from canonical single-shot BenchCAD, where the model receives one turn and must return its proposed code without an iterative render-and-repair loop.

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: Figure 7: Tool-crafted lookup commands reused across task in Task008. The task (top) asks for reimbursement claim whose evidence lives in mail client and bank account; the screenshot below it is the banks transactions tab after the agents own search tool has typed CATHAY. The agent writes mail open info.py and vault search.py once (middle) and invokes them 13 times with the arguments shown (bottom), once per supporting e-mail and once per charge. The first model it produced captured the base, seven fins, and four mounting holes, but gave the fins rectangular tops. After rendering the result, the agent noticed that each reference fin showed three top edges while its model showed only two. The agent tested triangular roof, one-sided chamfer, and symmetric chamfers. Only the symmetric chamfers reproduced the missing edge pattern. It then varied the fin height, thickness, length, spacing, chamfer size, base thickness, and hole radius, rendering and inspecting each candidate before choosing the next change. The run used 249 model turns and 67 image inspections. The agent executed the final program, rendered the resulting STEP file, inspected it, and submitted it. The official BenchCAD scorer returned voxel IoU 1.0000. The first guess was incomplete; execution and visual feedback exposed the missing feature and enabled the correction.

sections.title: Preprints
sections.content: A.6 DIRECT AND MULTI-AGENT EXECUTION ON OSWORLD We also examine how CUAWright fares under direct and multi-agent execution on OSWorld 2.0. Both conditions used GPT-5.6 Sol at maximum reasoning effort, the same benchmark release and task evaluator, and 300-step ceiling. In direct execution, one Actor owns the complete loop of inspection, editing, verification, and submission. In multi-agent execution, the Actor shares the step budget with Binder that extracts requirements, Critic that identifies risks or defects, and Verifier that decides whether the result is ready to submit; submission requires its final ready decision. We present two paired tasks with opposite outcomes: one in which multi-agent review changed and improved the artifact, and one in which direct execution was more effective. The examples illustrate how the two modes differ in practice rather than estimate their average performance. Table 8: Paired direct and multi-agent traces. Task 045: multi-agent advantage Task 076: direct advantage Task Record all seven dashboard pages in 1920 1080 GIF lasting at least five seconds and smaller than one MiB 0.95; 32 Actor steps; submitted 1.00; 129 total steps; submitted Direct Multi-agent Observed mechanism Critic changed the recording method Apply the speaker-note instructions across six slides, including layout, sensor, chart, workbook, and table edits 1.00; 42 Actor steps; submitted 0.95; 300 total steps; not submitted Repeated blocked submission inconclusive verification Task 045: multi-agent review improved the artifact. The task required promotional GIF that visited seven dashboard pages at 1920 1080, lasted at least five seconds, showed no obstructing desktop elements, and remained below one MiB. The direct Actor finished in 32 steps. It submitted seven-frame, 8.75-second GIF assembled from selected screenshots. The artifact covered every page and met the size and resolution requirements, but received half credit for frame count, for final score of 0.95. The multi-agent run used 35 Actor, 18 Binder, 12 Critic, and 64 Verifier steps. The Critic identified that small set of selected screenshots did not preserve the actual walkthrough and recommended genuine screen recording. The Actor then used byzanz-record while navigating the dashboard. The submitted GIF contained 156 frames, lasted 10.37 seconds, remained 5,168 bytes below one MiB, and scored 1.00. The report-to-action chain is visible, but the gain required 97 additional steps. Task 076: direct execution was more effective. The task required six presentation slides to be edited according to their speaker notes. The requested changes included title formatting, text-box spacing, movement of four sensor markers, an April chart and embedded-workbook update, deletion of temporary table, and alignment of every cell in budget table. The direct Actor completed the edits, reopened the file in WPS, checked the persistent package, submitted in 42 steps, and passed every criterion for score of 1.00. The multi-agent run used 198 Actor, 20 Binder, 30 Critic, and 52 Verifier steps. The Actor completed nearly all requested edits and final Critic found no concrete user-facing defect. Three Verifier calls nevertheless returned unknown. Because submission required final ready report, the run exhausted all 300 steps without submitting. Its persistent artifact scored 0.95; the only failed criterion was the Slide 2 body-box gap, which measured 228,600 EMU against 990,000-EMU threshold. The direct artifact measured 1,571,625 EMU. Task 045 shows where multi-agent review can justify its cost: the Critic identified specific artifact risk, the Actor changed its implementation, and the persistent result improved. Task 076 shows the opposite failure mode: review repeated without producing repair and consumed the budget needed for submission. The traces support Actor-first execution with specialist calls reserved for named uncertainties that imply concrete action.
